checks.hint: Type: set prior 0.01 -- the base rate of phishing.

expected_observations: With prior 1%, sensitivity 99%, FPR 5%, the posterior is ~0.167 -- the alert is real 1 time in 6.
Raising the prior to 20% (targeted campaign) jumps the posterior above 80% -- base rates dominate.
Lowering FPR to 1% helps more than raising sensitivity to 99.9% -- precision lives in the denominator.
labs.objective: Compute posterior alert probabilities with an interactive Bayes calculator on synthetic triage numbers.
steps: Open the Bayes Lab: a triage calculator with prior, sensitivity, and false-positive-rate dials.
Type: set prior 0.01, set sensitivity 0.99, set fpr 0.05.
Type: solve -- read the posterior P(phish | alert) and the natural-frequency explanation (per 10,000 emails).
Raise the prior to 0.20 (a targeted spear-phish campaign). Solve again -- observe the jump.
Reset prior to 0.01; lower fpr to 0.01. Solve -- compare against raising sensitivity to 0.999.
Write the rule: which knob buys the most precision per unit effort?
labs.success_message: Bayes computed, base-rate fallacy cured. You now multiply by the prior before trusting an alert.
labs.title: Bayes triage calculator

checks.hint: Type: set threshold 0.7 -- watch the confusion matrix update.
Type: show costs -- price each operating point.

expected_observations: The matrix updates live: precision, recall, F1 recompute per threshold.
Accuracy barely moves across thresholds -- it cannot see the tradeoff.
The minimum-loss threshold sits far from 0.50 under asymmetric costs.
labs.objective: Tune a threshold on synthetic scores and watch the confusion matrix, metrics, and expected loss move.
steps: Open the Confusion Lab: 2,000 synthetic scores, 5% malicious, cost model FP=$50 / FN=$50,000.
Type: set threshold 0.5, then show matrix -- record precision, recall, F1, accuracy.
Sweep the threshold 0.9 -> 0.1 in steps. Note which metric barely moves (accuracy) and which swing wildly.
Type: show costs at each step -- find the minimum expected-loss threshold.
Compare your optimum to 0.50. Write down the precision/recall pair economics chose.
labs.success_message: Matrix mastered, costs priced. Thresholds are now arithmetic, not habit.
labs.title: Confusion-matrix and threshold tuner

checks.hint: Type: set lr 0.1 -- a stable step size.
Type: step 5 -- watch x descend the bowl.
Type: reset -- back to the start for the divergence demo.

expected_observations: lr=0.9: fast descent with visible oscillation.
lr=1.1: overshoot grows each step -- divergence, not learning.
labs.objective: Visualize gradient descent on a quadratic bowl and discover the learning-rate stability boundary.
steps: Open the Gradient Lab: f(x) = x^2 rendered as a bowl, ball at x=4.
Type: set lr 0.1, then step 5 -- watch the ball roll downhill, steps shrinking.
Type: reset, set lr 0.9, step 5 -- faster, with oscillation.
Type: reset, set lr 1.1, step 5 -- watch the overshoot grow: divergence.
Find the largest stable lr by bisection (hint: stability needs lr < 1 for this bowl).
Write the rule: what does divergence look like, and what is the first knob you turn?
labs.success_message: Descent visualized, divergence demystified. Learning rate is now a stability knob, not a mystery.
labs.title: Gradient-descent visualizer
